assignments.title: VR Activity: Along the Line
assignments.html:
VR ACTIVITY
Along the Line
Solo · one in-headset session
16 points · file upload or text entry
❁ ✦ ❁
Before you start

Finish both lessons and read both sources first. Your notes from each page are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the page, so open it before you write. Then write your answers and submit them in this assignment.

WHAT YOU'RE DOING

By the winter of 1914 a line of trenches ran almost four hundred miles across France and Belgium, and neither side could break it. In your VR headset you will walk through a reconstruction of a Western Front trench system and the ground in front of it. Your task is to find evidence in the layout that helps explain why attacks so often failed.

WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset, charged and ready
▶
Your course page for this week, which lists the session link and the place to enter
▶
A notebook or open document for quick notes while you are in the session
▶
About 45 minutes in one sitting
HOW TO JOIN
Where to go: Open your immersive session from the link on your course page, then enter the location named there.
Solo or group: Solo. You do not need a partner.
If something fails: Write down what happened and use the help contact on your course page. Do not skip the activity.
WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Review first. Reread the section of the lesson “Trenches and a World at War” called Life and Death in the Trenches. Remember the barbed wire, the machine guns, the artillery, and the open ground of no man's land.
2
Walk the line. Start in the rear trenches and move forward to the front line, the way a soldier would on the way to an attack. Notice how the trenches are laid out and how they connect to each other.
3
Look across no man's land. Stand at the front trench and look at the ground between the two sides. Judge how far an attacker would have to cross in the open and what stands in the way.
4
Stop at three places. Choose three spots where the layout helps explain why a defender had the advantage. At each one, capture a picture with your headset and jot a note about what you see.
5
Listen for the soldier. At each spot, ask what a soldier who stood there would have seen, heard, and feared. Remember that you are visiting a reconstruction, and that real men lived and died in places like this.
6
Write your response. After you leave the session, write one paragraph of about 150 to 200 words that answers this question: How does the layout of the trenches help explain why attacks so often failed, and what can a reconstruction never tell you about what the soldiers went through?
WHAT TO SUBMIT

Submit your three captured images and your paragraph in the Canvas assignment. Use the images as evidence in your writing, and name which picture you are referring to.

Estimated time: 45 minutes

SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I walked from the rear trenches to the front line and looked out across no man's land.
☐
I captured three images that show different parts of the trench system.
☐
My paragraph uses at least two of my images as evidence.
☐
My paragraph connects what I saw to what I read about the trenches in the lesson “Trenches and a World at War”.
☐
I wrote in complete sentences and kept to about 150 to 200 words.
FACILITATOR NOTE

Teacher-facing. Before releasing this activity, add the session link and the specific location to the course page, and confirm that students have a way to capture images in their headsets. The instructions above assume a walkable reconstruction of a Western Front trench system. If none is available, substitute another reconstruction of the period and adjust the steps and review section to match, and note the substitution in the teacher's manual. The instructions are platform-neutral on purpose. Grade with the course rubric for VR activities: three images as evidence, a paragraph that cites them, and reasoning tied to the lesson.

quizzes.title: Module Intro: The Great War
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRO
The Great War
2 questions · survey · one attempt
❁ ✦ ❁
Essential question for this week
How did a murder in Sarajevo lead to a world war within six weeks, and could the war have been prevented?
Instructions

Welcome to The Great War. This short check-in is not graded. Your answers help your teacher see where each student is starting, so answer honestly.

What you will be able to do

The Road to 1914: Alliances, Arms, and Sarajevo

  • Describe how the alliance system and the arms race divided Europe into two camps.
  • Explain how the assassination at Sarajevo led to war within six weeks.
  • Evaluate which decisions of July 1914 might have been made differently.

Trenches and a World at War

  • Describe why the war on the Western Front became a stalemate of trenches.
  • Explain how the U-boat campaign and the Russian Revolution changed the war in 1917.
  • Evaluate how the war ended and what it destroyed.

discussions.title: Discussion: Could the July Crisis Have Been Stopped?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Could the July Crisis Have Been Stopped?
The Great War
10 points · threaded discussion
❁ ✦ ❁
Before you start

Finish both lessons first. Your notes from each lesson are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the lesson, so open it before you post. Then post your answer here and reply to one classmate.

DISCUSSION PROMPT

Within six weeks of the shooting at Sarajevo, Europe was at war. The lesson names several points where someone could have chosen differently: Germany by restraining Austria, Austria by accepting Serbia's reply, Russia by waiting, and Britain by speaking more clearly at the start. The alliances, the arms race, and the war plans also pressed on every decision.

Take a position. Could the July Crisis have been stopped? Support your position with at least two specific details from the lessons, and include one detail that points the other way. Explain why you weigh the evidence as you do.

Aim for about 150 to 200 words.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a detail from the lessons that they did not use. If not, explain respectfully where it falls short, and point to a detail from the lessons that supports your view.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
Criteria Substantive (full credit) Thin (partial credit) Missing (no credit)
Claim and evidence
5 pts		 Takes a clear position, supports it with at least two specific details from the lessons, and deals fairly with a detail that points the other way. Takes a position but gives only one detail, or stays general, or ignores the opposing detail. No post, or no clear position.
Response to a classmate
5 pts		 Answers a specific point in a classmate's post and either strengthens it with a new detail or explains politely where it falls short. Replies in general terms, such as agreeing or disagreeing without a detail from the lessons. No reply.
10 pts total
